Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, sour one week and true the next. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Lise had found the crack in March, reaching under the lid for a pencil. She showed Owen Dorran, the caretaker, and Nell passed the news to Mrs. Garvey within the week. Abel saw it for the first time now: a hairline split in the board that had opened since the last entry in the notebook of his old teacher, Tobias Rusk. For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch at each October tuning since, at the committee's expense. Lise had learned on it.

Nell's list caught his eye. She had noted each day the piano went sour, and when Abel struck a match on the stove's door to see the page, the dates were the coldest of the winter, the days the stove had roared. In November the committee had moved the piano from its corner to beside the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. He and Owen rolled it back to its corner.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel tapped the list. 'It's ready, and this did it. Thirty years of Rusk's notes and my own, and it took your dates to show me the stove.' He copied her list into the notebook under Rusk's last entry and wrote her name beside it.

On Saturday the stove roared across the room, and Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note. Mrs. Garvey's new piano was never ordered; her money went to a guard for the stove instead. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring true to the last chord.

Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, dull in the bass and quick to slip. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Tobias Rusk, Abel's old teacher, had first seen the crack thirty years ago and written it into his notebook: 'hairline split in the board, two inches, watch it.' In March Lise pointed it out again, Owen Dorran, the caretaker, measured it, and Nell passed the news to Mrs. Garvey. Rusk had always tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch each October since Rusk died, at the committee's expense. Lise had learned on it.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. But the split now ran the width of the board, and a tuning held there for a week at most. It struck Abel, running his thumb along it, that Rusk had known from the start how this would end. He tuned it anyway, note by note, at Rusk's pitch, for one more evening.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel kept his hand on the lid. 'For Saturday, yes. You should have heard this bass twenty years ago. It rang like a bell, and the whole hall hummed with it. That's gone now, and tuning won't fetch it back.' He pressed the low C once and listened to it fade.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note, and the old piano held for one evening more. Mrs. Garvey's new piano was to arrive on Monday, and Owen had cleared a space for it. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring short and dull on the final chord.

For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch at each October tuning since, at the committee's expense. Lise, who practised on the new piano at her school, heard it as flat.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. Lise wanted it at standard pitch for Saturday, though it would pull hard on the split. They struck a bargain: he would bring it up to standard pitch, and she would ring him at the first odd sound.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel kept his eyes on the split. 'Ready, yes. Keep the stove low and the doors shut till then, and ring me if you hear a crack like a pistol shot. I'll come at six on Saturday to check the board before anyone sits down.' He pencilled his number inside the lid.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme at standard pitch without a sour note, and the split held to the last chord. Mrs. Garvey's offer of a new piano stood, in case the board gave way later. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring bright and true.

Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, with a buzz somewhere in the bass. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Nell had found the crack in March, dusting under the lid, and she told Owen Dorran, the caretaker, then Lise, then Mrs. Garvey, all in one breathless afternoon. Abel saw it for the first time now: a hairline split in the board that had opened since the last entry in the notebook of his old teacher, Tobias Rusk. For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch at each October tuning since, at the committee's expense. Lise had learned on it.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel struck the low C, and the buzz came at once. One bass string had snapped near its pin, and the loose end lay rattling against its neighbours. He fitted a new string from his case and tuned it to match the rest, at Rusk's pitch.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel, who had shared a desk with her at school forty years before, held up the broken string between two fingers. 'In ten minutes. Here is the monster that sent you running to Mrs. Garvey. Shall we have it framed for the committee room?' He coiled it and dropped it into her palm with a little bow.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note, and the new string sat among the old ones as if it had always been there. Mrs. Garvey kept her money for a new piano another year. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring true on the final chord.

For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and that same week she opened a savings account for the carousel and began drafting letters to banks. Then she went looking for the families. It took her five years: buyers had moved, married and died, and one lot number led her through three counties. The first horse she brought home had hung outside a saddler's shop as a sign. After it, slowly, came horses from a school hall, a chapel basement, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back.

The rest went quickly. A raffle in 1993 paid for nearly all of the restoration, and the letters to the banks were never sent. Shown a photograph taken in 1923 of crowds around the carousel on the common, the council agreed in one evening that it should stand there again. The band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows, and the original colours showed plainly under later paint. One wet May morning, six men raised the canopy onto its centre pole.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought for Hal's sister, Edie. When Nora came to ask for it, Hal took her out to the barn and stood a long while beside the grey, running his thumb along its chipped mane and telling her about the summers Edie had ridden it on the common, years before she died. Then he went to fetch the trailer.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

The dispute ran through eleven meetings and two winters, until a councillor raised the matter of the common's drains and the yard won by one vote. By then the raffle, its tickets printed with a photograph taken in 1923 of the carousel in full swing, had sold out in a week and paid for the restoration. The band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows, and the original colours showed plainly under later paint.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Hal and Nora had sung side by side in the chapel choir for twenty years. When she asked for the grey, he told her she could have it if she could catch it, and led her to a stall where the wooden horse stood between his two real ones, wearing a halter, a bucket of oats at its feet. He hitched up the trailer that afternoon.

The carousel turned again in the station yard in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, a chapel basement and an ivied garden, until every horse but one was back.

For three years Nora and a retired chemist took the coats off a square inch at a time. The rest went quickly. A raffle raised four thousand pounds, which paid for the restoration; the band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows; and the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common, so the letter went unsent.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Sure of her welcome, Nora told the Courier the grey would be home by Easter before writing to Hal, and he read it there first. When she did ask, his answer was two lines: she might have asked a man before announcing his property in the paper, and she could come and discuss it once she had learned some manners.

The grey came home in June, after Nora drove out to the Brigg farm to apologise. The carousel turned again on the common that July, every horse in place.

For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

In August the Orsk Gazette ran a photograph of Vell holding an empty trap beside the new sand fence. The fence had gone up along the dune foot over the winter, its slats set close and sunk a hand deep. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir, and visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass.

Arkin spent his first two nights under the boardwalk lamps and tallied eleven beetles. It was Vell who thought of the fence. Her notebooks held sixteen years of sketched night tracks, and nearly all of them crossed the dune foot where the slats now stood. At dusk the two of them knelt by the fence and watched beetles climb its face, slide back, and climb again until the tide turned.

Arkin asked whether the beetles would find their old crossings once the fence was opened. Vell took down the photograph pinned above her desk, from her first summer: the dune foot at night, streaked with tracks all the way to the water. She looked at it a long time, then said she used to stand there in the dark just to hear them pass, and that the sound had been gone since the slats went up.

Vell asked the park to cut gaps in the fence, a hand wide and ten metres apart. This July the count came back to five hundred and ninety.

At Vell's request the park roped off the north hollow in August. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass; this July the count was already six hundred and ten.

Vell left the traps and the spit exactly as they were. This July, with the fence, the lamps and the visitors all still there, the count climbed back to seven hundred and forty.
